material.title: Introduction to Linear Combinations
material.summary: Covers vector scaling and addition, the concept of linear combination, and how to determine whether a target vector can be expressed as a combination of given vectors.
learning_objectives: Understand how vectors can be scaled by scalar coefficients.
Understand how scaled vectors can be combined through addition.
Determine whether a target vector lies within the span of given vectors.
Solve for scalar coefficients that produce a required linear combination.

concepts.name: Linear Combination
concepts.definition: A linear combination of vectors v₁, v₂, … vₙ is an expression of the form c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ + … + cₙvₙ, where c₁…cₙ are scalar coefficients.
principles: A vector can be scaled by multiplying each of its components by a scalar.
Two scaled vectors can be added component-wise.
Any vector in the span of a set can be expressed as a linear combination.
methods: Set up a system of equations: c₁ * v₁ + c₂ * v₂ = target.
Solve for c₁ and c₂ using substitution or elimination.
Verify by substituting back into the original equation.
misconceptions: Confusing scalar multiplication with dot product.
Assuming all vectors can always be combined to produce any target.
source_evidence: A linear combination of vectors v₁ and v₂ is defined as c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ for scalars c₁ and c₂.
If a target vector t can be expressed as c₁v₁ + c₂v₂, then t is in the span of {v₁, v₂}.

concepts.name: Vector Span
concepts.definition: The span of a set of vectors is the set of all possible linear combinations of those vectors.
principles: Two non-parallel vectors in ℝ² span the entire plane.
Parallel vectors only span a single line.
methods: Determine if a target vector can be written as a linear combination.
Check whether the coefficient system has a consistent solution.
misconceptions: Assuming more vectors always produce a larger span.
Confusing span with the set of vectors themselves.
source_evidence: The span of {v₁, v₂} is the set {c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ | c₁, c₂ ∈ ℝ}.

scope_limitations: This material does not cover vector spaces with more than two dimensions.
Matrix notation and operations are not covered.

material.title: Introduction to Matrix Transformations
material.summary: Covers how matrices act on vectors as linear transformations, and how composition corresponds to matrix multiplication.
learning_objectives: Interpret a matrix as a linear transformation of vectors.
Compute the image of a vector under a matrix transformation.
Compose two transformations by multiplying their matrices.

concepts.name: Matrix Transformation
concepts.definition: A matrix A of size m×n defines a linear transformation T(x) = Ax mapping vectors in ℝⁿ to vectors in ℝᵐ.
principles: Matrix-vector multiplication applies the transformation encoded by the matrix.
Linear transformations map the zero vector to the zero vector and preserve scalar sums.
methods: Multiply each row of the matrix by the input vector and sum the products.
Test linearity by checking T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v) and T(cu) = cT(u).
misconceptions: Assuming every vector always has a preimage under a given matrix.
source_evidence: For a matrix A and vector x, the map x → Ax is linear.

scope_limitations: Determinants and eigenvalues are not covered.

material.title: Introduction to Probability Distributions
material.summary: Covers discrete probability distributions, their expected value, and the conditions a valid distribution must satisfy.
learning_objectives: Identify the requirements for a valid discrete probability distribution.
Compute the expected value of a discrete random variable.

concepts.name: Discrete Probability Distribution
concepts.definition: A discrete probability distribution assigns a probability p(x) ≥ 0 to each possible value of a discrete random variable, with all probabilities summing to 1.
principles: Probabilities are non-negative and sum to one across all outcomes.
Expected value is the probability-weighted sum of all outcomes.
methods: Verify that all probabilities sum to exactly 1 before using a distribution.
Compute E[X] = Σ x·p(x) over all outcomes x.
misconceptions: Assuming a distribution is valid solely because all probabilities are individually less than 1.
source_evidence: A valid discrete distribution satisfies p(x) ≥ 0 and Σ p(x) = 1.

scope_limitations: Continuous distributions and conditional probability are not covered.
